'Abstract' section.text:
A production loop needs explicit stopping conditions rather than an unbounded graph run. [3]

This paper separates a reference implementation's three exits from the turn and recursion limits documented by two agent runtimes. [1][2][3]

'Introduction' section.text:
An agent loop is a program that calls a model, acts on the reply, and repeats. The repetition is useful only when its stopping boundary is explicit. [3]

Deep Agents documents a recursion limit as the graph boundary. [3] This is a single source documentation statement, so it is a runtime detail rather than a general result.

'Exit conditions' section.text:
The Sol3 reference implementation checks three exits in order: done, cost, then max turns. [1] This is a design policy in the reference implementation, not a claim that vendors standardize the same three conditions.

The Claude Agent SDK exposes a turn cap as `max_turns`, while Deep Agents documents a recursion limit. [2][3] Each runtime detail rests on a single source and should be read as documented behavior for that runtime.

'Independent verification' section.text:
The agent-loop guidance says verification works best when the verifier does not share the actor's context. [4] CRITIC likewise reports that intrinsic self-correction without external feedback rarely improves correctness. [5]

Together these sources motivate a structural maker/checker split. The conclusion about any specific tool scope is an engineering inference, not a measured result in these sources. [4][5]

'Limitations' section.text:
This paper combines one reference implementation, two runtime documents, and one paper on self-correction. [1][2][3][5] It measures no production loops and reports no cost figures of its own.

The runtime limits are each single source observations. Treat them as documented behavior for those runtimes, not as a universal property of agent systems. [2][3]
